messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Megan is 19, recently married, and unemployed, living with her husband in a small apartment where most evenings now feel organized around safety. When she describes the assault, she does so in fragments that come back with startling force rather than as a steady story. It happened after dark, on a night she can date exactly and has never been able to approach easily since. She had been outside in an area where motorcycles passed nearby and where raised male voices carried from the street. What remains most vivid to her are not broad outlines but sensory pieces that still seem to arrive fully formed: the revving of a motorcycle engine, shouting in Arabic, and the heavy smell of alcohol close to her. When those details are stirred in the present, Megan does not experience them as distant reminders. She says the whole scene can come back “all at once,” without warning, as if she is there again.

In the weeks after the assault, she found herself scanning constantly. At home, she began listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering the apartment. Ordinary building noises would pull her upright in bed, her attention fixed on the door, the hallway, the windows. If someone moved in the corridor outside, she was immediately alert, trying to identify whether the sound signaled danger. When she did have to leave home, she kept looking behind her to check whether someone was following. She could not relax into a walk or a short errand; her body stayed braced, her head turning over her shoulder again and again. At times, when a motorcycle passed or when she caught the smell of alcohol on a stranger, she would suddenly feel as though the assault were happening again. In those moments she was no longer just remembering. She would hear in her head the same sounds from that night, including the shouting, and sometimes she could smell the alcohol as if it were present around her again.

Because the memories arrived this way, Megan began narrowing her life. She stopped going out at night and became firm about being indoors before dark. If plans ran late, she canceled them. As the anniversary of the assault approached, she avoided the date altogether, refusing conversations about that time and trying not to look at calendars. She has come to treat certain days as dangerous simply because they are connected to what happened. Another change has been harder for her to speak about. Since the assault, paying attention to her own body has felt unbearable. She avoids looking at her body and tries not to notice physical details about herself. Even routine moments like getting dressed or passing a mirror can become something she rushes through. She does not describe this as vanity or embarrassment; it feels to her more like something she cannot bear to face.

These habits have shaped her marriage and daily life. Because she is unemployed, she spends long stretches at home, where the apartment is both refuge and place of vigilance. Her husband has seen how quickly an evening can change when motorcycle noise rises from the street below, or when voices outside sound angry and unfamiliar. He has also watched her retreat from ordinary activities after sunset. Their world has grown smaller. She notices that this is not how she imagined married life beginning, and this recognition is painful in its own right.

What Megan says has changed most is her understanding of the world and of herself. She had once assumed there were basic rules—that people were mostly understandable, that danger had limits, that if she was careful enough she could move through life safely. Now she says those beliefs have been destroyed. The world no longer feels ordered to her, only unpredictable and suddenly threatening. Alongside this is a harsh judgment about herself. She has come to believe she is no longer capable of the things that used to define her. At 19, those defining things were ordinary but important: being able to go where she needed, tolerate being out in the world, trust her own responses. She compares herself constantly to an imagined other person, someone who “would have stopped it,” and feels certain that somebody else would have coped better, fought harder, done something decisive that she could not do.

By the time she sought help, the strain of living this way had become difficult to ignore. The immediate reason was not one single symptom but the accumulation of them: the apartment feeling like a place she had to guard, the nights closed off, the startle and reliving when a motorcycle passed, the dread of the approaching date on the calendar, the sense that even her own body had become something to avoid. What frightened her most was the possibility that this was now permanent—that the world would always feel ruined and that she would always be the person who could not stop what happened. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the memory but to stop being overtaken by it without warning and to feel capable of inhabiting her life again.
